result.scope_note: The text describes a software release event involving royalty-free reuse terms.

explanation.text: CERN released World Wide Web software into the public domain on April 30, 1993, enabling royalty-free reuse, as confirmed by CERN's own licensing page and multiple sources spanning the event date and purpose.

CERN's 30 April 1993 statement explicitly placed the three core Web components (line‑mode client, basic server, common code library) in the Public Domain, relinquishing all IP rights and granting permission to use, duplicate, modify, and distribute royalty‑free.

The 1993 public domain release was followed by CERN's 1994 open‑source transition, where CERN retained copyright but granted perpetual, irrevocable royalty‑free use rights, clarifying the licensing evolution.

excerpts.text:
First, one has to determine if he was an employee hired to do something like invent the WWW. He "spent time" at CERN, but was an independent contractor in his first period (1980), then took up a fellowship in 1984. "Fellowship" is generally not an "employment" relationship in the relevant sense, and academics are rarely "employees" in the common law work-for-hire sense. It is [reported](http://www.governingwithcode.org/case_studies/pdf/NCSAmosaic.pdf) that he "began creating the software and standards for the web on his own as an informal project within CERN". So if anyone holds IP rights (to what?), it would be him.

Given where CERN is, it is not self-evident whose copyright law would be applicable. [He reports](https://www.w3.org/People/Berners-Lee/FAQ.html#cernoffice) that he wrote the code in CERN Building 31, which appears to be in France, though CERN appears to be in Switzerland (CERN is, in fact, in France and Switzerland). [Article 17](https://www.admin.ch/opc/en/classified-compilation/19920251/index.html#a17) of Swiss copyright law says

> Where a computer program has been created under an employment contract in the course of discharging professional duties or fulfilling contractual obligations, the employer alone shall be entitled to exercise the exclusive rights of use.

excerpts.text:
On 30 April 1993 CERN issued a public statement stating that the three components of Web software (the basic line-mode client, the basic server and the library of common code) were put in the Public Domain with the statement:

CERN relinquishes all intellectual property rights to this code, both source and binary and permission is given to anyone to use, duplicate, modify and distribute it.
